body.text: I’ve been playing computer games since I was a kid, so when “Shift at Midnight” came out in August and quickly became one of the hottest games on social media, I had to give it a try. It is a cooperative horror game in which players work the night shift at a supermarket. Players have to identify customers who are monsters in disguise, keep the supermarket running, and, of course, fight the monsters after nightfall. According to the game developers, this game is best suited for three players, so I needed two teammates.

The easy option would be to find teammates in the game lobby. But as an introvert and also not-so-skilled player, I feel very reluctant to team up with strangers. In team games, a simple mistake can lead to failures and that means upsetting other players. Teammates easily lose patience and start pressuring each other. I hate the blaming and yelling; they really take all the fun out of the game.

So I found my teammates another way. I decided to hire two gaming companions through DONGDONG E-GAME, a platform dedicated to this type of gaming companion service that I had come across through their livestreams and promo videos on social media. I paid around 40 to 50 yuan ($6-7) per person per hour. They both seemed to be recent college graduates. And judging from our in-game conversation, I think they were treating this as a full-time job.

Our game lasted five hours. I got to play at the checkout, where I tried to identify suspicious customers; this was the most fun part of the game. My companions took care of cleaning, stocking goods, and most of the fighting. One was particularly familiar with the game and knew where the monsters would appear. He would warn me before the more frightening scenes.

After hours spotting monsters and fighting spiders, we finally reached the big boss, and I died within seconds (in my defense, that was one hell of a boss fight). They finished the fight while I sat and watched our battle. The game ended. We had earned enough money to save our pet cat, one of the desired outcomes, but we failed to save a police officer who was eventually killed by the monster. This is one of the “bad endings,” but I was okay with it.
Paying for someone to play a video game with you may sound strange. I also imagine many people would laugh at the idea of taking on this kind of work as a career.

How much you pay really depends on the type of gaming companion you want. There are two types: skill-based companionship and entertainment companionship. Skill-based companionship is for people who want a skilled teammate to help them win or achieve a particular objective. If they lose or fail to achieve the objective then they will give a conditional refund or some make-up sessions. For the more popular competitive games such as “Delta Force” or “Valorant,” I’ve seen hourly rates ranging from 60 yuan to as high as 500 yuan, depending on the skill of the player and the nature of the service.
Entertainment companionship is for people who just want some company, some light chatting, and an enjoyable gaming experience. That’s exactly what I got in my paid session.
When Intimacy Becomes the Product

Gaming companions make some sense to me. The session has clear goals: to win a game or at least enjoy the game. But there are other types of paid companions in today’s Chinese society, with more focus on intimacy.

One good example is lianpei, paid love role-playing games, which is a niche product in the bigger sector of jubensha, the immersive role-playing games popular among Chinese young people for quite some time. A typical romance role-play session normally involves six to 10 people, including one or two dungeon masters (DMs). The rest are players who pay to participate. DMs are performers hired by the venue to perform roles and interact with players. The game enacts romance stories filled with passion, jealousy, separation, and reconciliation. There is limited physical intimacy such as holding hands and hugging, or maybe a light kiss on the forehead.

A classical immersive role-playing game session usually costs a little over 100 yuan per person, but romantic role-play sessions can easily cost 200 to 300 yuan per person or more. Some players said they have spent over 1,000 yuan to make one session happen.

As anyone can easily imagine, DMs are usually good looking charming young people, and popular ones can easily attract their own fans. Players need to secure booking weeks or even months in advance, and sometimes they need to pay extra for it. In some extreme cases, players would cover most or even the entire cost of the group to make sure they can book the script and the DM they want. This reminds me of idol culture in Asia. Idols’ popularity usually depends on their interaction and connections with fans.

In August 2026, Chinese media reported a very concerning case involving lianpei. A 16-year-old girl in Shanghai reportedly spent around 170,000 yuan on romantic role-play sessions. According to the news report, she had booked hundreds of sessions at the same venue over the last two years. Her family accused the venue of encouraging her to keep spending.

This is an extreme case, but it reveals how much greed and tragedy can be associated with this type of transaction. Both gaming companions and DMs tend to describe what they do as a service. They make this sound like a very strict business transaction, where customers pay for and receive a specific service.

However, feelings are never that simple and straightforward; they are unpredictable and sometimes stubborn. On a rational level, the players know this is a scripted love session that they paid money to join. They know the person playing their lover or friend is just doing their job, and still, players fall for them from time to time, over and over again.
The Business of Being Wanted

Attempting to purchase intimacy is not new. Paying for companionship, sex, matchmaking, and the attention of others is a phenomenon as old as recorded history. The psychology behind these transactions is actually quite simple. We want to feel wanted and we want to believe that we are special to someone. We want to feel loved.

In Chinese classical literature, many stories about courtesans and their patrons share this theme. They tend to examine the thin lines between money, sex, and genuine affection. A recurring theme is that what begins as a transaction might eventually lead to true love. In a very well-known Ming Dynasty story, the heroine Du Shiniang, a young courtesan, falls in love with a young man who has a promising career. Du intends to leave the brothel and start a new life with him. When another man comes along and offers money for her however, her lover immediately agrees to sell her.

The story ends in tragedy, with Du Shiniang throwing her treasure chest into the river and ending her own life. She genuinely believed she could walk away from her past and that her lover was actually in love with her – not her reputation, not her money, but her as a person. In the end, however, he felt money mattered the most.

The story may be hundreds of years old but the core theme still resonates. The quest for true affection has not stopped; on the contrary, now in the internet age, with the help of new technology, this age-old search is taking new commercial forms. On Chinese streaming platforms such as Douyin and Kuaishou, many talented (or not) hosts sing, dance, or simply chat with viewers, hoping to receive virtual gifts. In a random group hosts’ livestream, I have seen one viewer sending ten Carnivals (worth 3,000 yuan each) in just five seconds.

This is also where things can become very ugly. Some livestreaming hosts actively encourage these gifts, and imply to viewers that spending more will bring them closer. The viewers keep spending money, hoping to prove that their relationship means something more than business. Chinese media have reported cases of viewers spending hundreds of thousands of yuan, even up to millions on livestream hosts they may never have met in person.

This serves as the underlying logic for almost all companion businesses. The key is to make customers feel there is a special connection to the person they pay. The more they believe in that idea, the more they spend. With the help of new technology, it has become so much easier to access people and sustain the illusion of closeness; all you need is a smartphone and internet access.

During my research for this article, I have encountered too many stories of people spending a lot to chase the slightest hope of pursuing true love. The reporting on these alarming cases is full of anger and regret, with customers saying they had been cheated and manipulated.

After reading a particularly disturbing case of someone spending millions, I found myself asking: should I sympathize because there was clearly manipulation and fraud involved, or should I just write them off as stupid and gullible?

In the end, the desire for love is not generated by the internet or any other technological set-up. It is so fundamental, it feels part of who we are, rooted in our heart. Is it so wrong for people to seek true affection, even under these circumstances? It’s particularly hard to ignore that pull when the other party is continually giving you reasons to stay in the relationship, even a toxic one.
In the companionship industry, service has a price, and the transaction ends when the session is over. However, the feelings it produces do not obey these boundaries.
